title: Maneuver warfare and the OODA loop
note: Attrition warfare wins by wearing down the enemy's forces; maneuver warfare tries to shatter the enemy's cohesion through speed, surprise and attacks on weakness. US Air Force colonel John Boyd described conflict as a contest of decision cycles, Observe, Orient, Decide, Act, in which the side that cycles faster and orients better pulls the rival into confusion.

read.title: Faster loops
text: John Boyd flew fighters for the US Air Force and later taught air combat, where he noticed that the winner was often the pilot who could change what he was doing faster than his opponent could follow. He generalized the idea into a loop of four steps: observe the situation, orient to it, decide, and act. Every person and organization runs this loop, and each action changes the situation, so the loop begins again.

Boyd argued that the side able to run the loop faster, and with better orientation, gains a growing advantage. Orientation is the heart of the loop: our culture, training, past experience and analysis shape what we notice and how we interpret it. An opponent whose picture of events keeps falling behind reality acts on outdated assumptions, grows confused and may finally lose cohesion altogether.

This thinking fed the doctrine of maneuver warfare, which seeks to win by disrupting an enemy's system rather than by grinding down every unit. It favors speed, surprise, attacks on weakness rather than strength, and subordinates trusted to act on their commander's intent. Businesses and sports teams borrowed the same idea: the competitor who learns and adapts fastest often wins.
